name: Example: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/19b420204caf7f2706b4d355b5538dc347b5377d2b9f99297dbf6accc3220f59.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = \theta,$ shown above.
worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=\theta,$ we get

$$
x = \theta\cos\theta, \qquad y=\theta\sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
